newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC - consensus doesn't mean community.
newsitem.headline: APEC - consensus doesn't mean community.

text.p: A joke going the rounds at the annual conference of Asia-Pacific nations goes: What does APEC stand for? A Perfect Excuse for Chatting.
APEC is, of course, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation -- four adjectives in search of a noun, in the timeless description of former Australia Foreign Minister Gareth Evans.

An Australian brainchild, the 18-member group at its inception in 1989 rejected putting "community" in its name in favour of the fuzzier "cooperation" to emphasize it was not going to be a trade bloc or a Pacific version of the European Community.

APEC's reluctance since then to take unequivocal stands on issues, or bolder steps to achieve its vision of a Pacific basin free trade area from Tasmania to Alaska and China to Chile, has fostered its image as one of the world's leading talking shops.
But U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher told a news conference in Manila the talks have value.

"These meetings afford an opportunity for our foreign and trade ministers to come together to exhange views, to forge a new consensus on various issues, to move forward to shape the Pacific community and draw all of our economies closer together."
But in what is viewed as a blow to U.S. diplomacy, APEC ministers this year declined to endorse Washington's proposal to eradicate tariffs on information technology equipment by the year 2000.

Instead, the trade and foreign ministers said they endorsed continuing negotiations about an information technology agreement (ITA) in Geneva and hoped one could be concluded at the inaugural World Trade Organisation meeting next month in Singapore.
"APEC can only go as fast as its most reluctant member," said one senior official, referring to the group's decision-making based on consensus.
That would be Malaysia, a rapidly developing country which has long harboured suspicions that APEC is striving to become something more than a vehicle for cooperation.
Malaysia at this meeting argued for "flexibility" in meeting ITA targets and emphasised any commitments made in APEC about the pact would be strictly voluntary.
"We can support it only to the extent that it doesn't hurt us," Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad told a news conference.

It was Malaysia which insisted on inserting language in the APEC's landmark "Bogor Declaration" two years ago in Indonesia that the commitment to create a free trade by the year 2020 was non-binding on individual members.

APEC enthusiasts look at the group's astonishing economic numbers and see power: the 18 countries constitute nearly half the world's population; at $16 trillion, they own 55 percent of global income; they represent more than 40 percent of world trade.

APEC sceptics look at the sheer diversity of the group and see contradictions: it embraces practically all the world's religions, dozens of languages, and is home to an astonishing mix of peoples and lifestyles from Australia's aborigines to California's yuppies.
The enthusiasts argue for "a level playing field" in which all the players operate under the same rules for what U.S. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor calls "mutually assured prosperity".
The sceptics, led by Mahathir, say a level playing field is still unfair if "on one side of the field you have giants and on the other side you have pygmies".
Still, APEC has taken a number of small steps to forge links.
At the ministerial meeting, members presented "action plans" to dismantle trade barriers. Many merely summarised measures they had already taken in recent months. Some unveiled new initiatives.
A joint ministerial declaration called the plans a "credible beginning."
Three members -- Australia, Korea and the Philippines -- said they would introduce a business travel card to facilitate travel among members.
"The group is more incremental than monumental," one official quipped.
